newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Luxembourg financial market losing ground.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg financial market losing ground.

text.p: Luxembourg has peaked as a financial services centre and its capacity for further growth in the face of growing competition from other centres such as London and Dublin is limited, local bankers say.

The likely introduction of the single currency in 1999 as part of Europe's economic and monetary union and accompanying harmonisation measures will remove competitive advantages which have made Luxembourg an attractive location for niche players.
Luxembourg bankers are intensively looking for new areas and new products to safeguard the Grand Duchy's position as an offshore centre for financial services.

"We are looking for potential for new niches," Ekkehard Storck, managing director of Deutsche Bank Luxembourg SA -- a wholly-owned subsidiary of Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank -- told a news conference on Wednesday.
His remarks had been embargoed for publication on Friday.
One such product could be pension funds, he said. The Luxembourg Banking Association ABBL had already defined the shape of such a product, which would be marketed across borders.
Now a legal framework needed to be created, Storck said, including accords on double taxation in Luxembourg and the buyer's country of origin and a supervisory framework.
The right fiscal and legal framework would also have to be in place in important markets such as Germany to give the product a place in a country's overall pension system.

Returning to Luxembourg's performance, Storck said that in 1996 growth had slowed in the euro market loans business and private banking. The latter suffered from the impact on Luxembourg's image of various judicial probes in Germany and Belgium into tax evasion and Luxembourg bank accounts.

The aggregate balance sheet total of Luxembourg banks rose by 3.9 percent in the first 10 months of 1996 to 926 billion marks, Storck said, quoting figures from the Luxembourg Monetary Institute (central bank).
The number of banks was steady at around 220, of which 72 were German-owned banks, making up the largest contingent from one single country.

The workforce in the financial services sector grew by 400 to 20,485, with the percentage of foreign employees rising to 59 from 58. The sector accounts for over nine percent of jobs in the Grand Duchy.
Aggregate profits before provisions rose by 6.8 percent, helped by buoyant markets and growth in fee income and profits from proprietary trading. Net interest income was lower.
The key euro credit market was stagnant.
"Euro credit market growth lagged that of the bond market," Storck said.

Quoting figures from the Bank for International Settlements, he said total lending in foreign currencies inside European countries rose by 3.5 percent in the first nine months of 1996 to about $420 billion, but Luxembourg's market share slipped from 12.5 percent to 11.8 percent.
The bulk of the euro market loans and deposits was in marks, with the dollar the second largest currency.

The mark's prominence still reflects German banks having moved business out of Germany to Luxembourg to evade German minimum reserve requirements. No interest is paid on such reserves deposited with the Bundesbank.

Storck said that in EMU minimum reserve requirements would be harmonised, removing this reason for German banks to export business and wiping out one of the attractions for German banks to bank in Luxembourg.

As he did last year, Storck again called for Luxembourg to cut the tax burden on companies, adding that recent measures to lower it to 39 percent from above 40 percent were a step in the right direction.

Deutsche Bank AG board member and outgoing DB Lux supervisory board chairman Ulrich Weiss noted that in the past years the bank had paid 1.3 billion marks in taxes to Luxembourg, roughly equalling the amount of profit paid to the parent bank in Frankfurt over the same period.

Noting the comparable tax burden in London was 33 percent and only 10 percent in Dublin's reduced-tax financial services centre, both Storck and Weiss said that tax considerations had gained in importance in view of the growing competition in banking and the resulting pressure on margins.

"As a result of the tax situation (in Luxembourg) a number of banks founded subsidiaries in Ireland, in the International Financial Services Centre in Dublin. Deutsche Bank Luxembourg can no longer ignore this trend," Storck said.
The bank has set up Deutsche Bank/DB Ireland plc with a capital of 200 million marks, mainly to refinance euro market credits. Operations are due to start in May.
